answer.rationale:
The 18% spend mandate makes memory_c2 (switch to low-cost vendor cut unit cost sharply) the most seductive and most load-bearing memory, so it is the one worth spending the single verification pull on. It is also the least safe to act on blind: it is dated 'last year', says nothing about performance under constrained allocation or at 94% committed volume, and 'onboarding was quick' was observed in some prior context we cannot see. A migration executed inside a 14-day window with zero line buffer converts a cost objective into a delivery-risk event, which directly violates the stated constraint of not increasing delivery risk. So I want the original record to see whether the cost win came with volume/lead-time conditions before letting it dominate.

My current intent is negotiate_terms. It is the only direction supported by two independent memories that both point at cost reduction without touching the supply path: memory_c4 (benchmarking moved the incumbent on price and payment terms) and memory_c6 (longer commitment unlocked volume pricing without narrowing service scope), with memory_c1 confirming the incumbent integration is stable and migration-free. That combination attacks TCO from the price and term side while leaving physical continuity intact, which is what a 94%-utilization line requires. It also composes: a renegotiated multi-year price is the baseline any future switch or second-source decision gets measured against, whereas a rushed switch destroys that baseline.

Risks I am carrying forward rather than resolving: negotiation alone may not reach a full 18%, so this could be a partial answer that defers the remainder to the next review; memory_c6's 'no narrowing of service scope' may not hold if we press harder on price this time, so scope language needs explicit protection in the term sheet. add_second_source (memory_c3) is genuinely valuable for resilience but spends the single decision slot on risk reduction rather than the mandated cost cut, and defer_decision (memory_c5) is inapplicable because this contract is critical and does not auto-renew — letting it lapse is the worst delivery outcome available. If verification shows memory_c2's cost win was unconditional and repeatable, I would still stage it as a small guarded qualification behind a renegotiated incumbent contract rather than a primary switch this cycle.
